findings.title: Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID slices
findings.body: The new batch logging in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) uses r.log.Error for normal, successful operation (e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`, where `err` is provably nil because it was already checked above). Since the cleanup job now runs every minute (see cleanup.go change) and each batch can contain up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs (the test exercises 32,767), this will emit error-level log lines containing potentially tens of thousands of IDs per batch, on every cycle, even when nothing is deleted (count 0). This floods logs, pollutes error metrics/alerting, and looks like a production failure. These should be Debug-level and should not include the full ID slice.

findings.title: Ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute multiplies frequency of ALL cleanup jobs, not just annotations
findings.body: Changing `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in CleanUpService.Run increases the run frequency of every job in `clean()` (expired snapshots, dashboard version deletion, expired image deletion, user invite expiry, short URL deletion, query history row-limit enforcement) by 10x, not just the annotation cleanup this PR targets. Additionally, `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so under load (e.g. the annotation cleanup processing many batches) a run can exceed the 1-minute tick interval; Go tickers buffer one tick, so the next cleanup starts immediately after the previous finishes, meaning cleanup jobs can effectively run back-to-back continuously against the database. This behavioral change is not mentioned in the PR description and should either be scoped to the annotation job or justified and documented.

findings.title: Only SQLite's parameter limit is special-cased; large batch sizes will fail on SQL Server and MySQL
findings.body: deleteByIDs generates one `?` placeholder per ID and only falls back to inlining literal values when the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999. Other supported databases have their own prepared-statement parameter limits (SQL Server: 2100, MySQL: 65,535). A user who configures `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above those limits (the test itself uses 32,767, which would exceed SQL Server's 2100 limit) will get hard failures from the DELETE on every cleanup cycle. The old single-statement DELETE with a subquery had no such parameter count. The guard should key off the actual dialect's parameter limit (or the actual len(ids)) rather than only SQLite's 999.

findings.title: O(n²) string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
findings.body: In the SQLite large-batch branch of deleteByIDs, the ID list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop, which copies the accumulated string on every iteration. For a batch of 32,767 IDs this allocates roughly megabytes of intermediate strings and is quadratic in the batch size. Use a strings.Builder (or a single fmt.Sprint of the slice) instead.
